subs: Kannapolis, North Carolina.
Wednesday, 30 July 2003.
That morning, the company that ran the mills here stopped.
4,340 people lost their jobs on the same day.
It was the largest single layoff in the history of the state.
For most of the century before, this town had no mayor,
no council and no city hall. It had a company.
The company owned the mill, and the houses the workers lived in.
Three years later, the mill itself came down.
This is the story of the town that made America's towels.
Who built it, who worked in it, and what happened when the looms stopped.
It begins seven miles to the south, in Concord.
In 1887, a merchant named James William Cannon organised a cotton mill there.
In 1898, his mills switched from plain cloth to towels.
They were the first towels ever made in the South.
Towels sold. So Cannon needed a bigger mill,
and a place to put the people who would run it.
In 1906, he bought about 800 acres of farmland,
on the old wagon road between Salisbury and Charlotte.
On those fields he built a mill, and around the mill, a town.
He asked the county to give it a name, starting with a K.
Kannapolis. You will often hear that it means “city of looms”.
Local historians are not so sure.
The likeliest meaning is the plainest one: Cannon's town.
The mill needed hands,
and the hands came from the farms, whole families at a time.
The machines were the same in every mill. Cotton went in at one end, as bales.
It was opened, cleaned, combed into ribbons, drawn out,
twisted into thread on spinning frames, wound onto bobbins, and woven on looms.
In Kannapolis, almost all of it became one thing.
Towels. And later, sheets.
By 1914, Cannon was making more towels and sheets than any company in the world.
In 1912, a photographer came to Kannapolis with a heavy camera and a notebook.
His name was Lewis Hine.
Hine worked for the National Child Labor Committee.
His job was to prove, with pictures, what children were doing in American factories.
He wrote down what the children told him.
Their names, their ages, and how long they had worked.
This is Herman Parker. The caption Hine wrote says:
“said six years old, and he and others said
he had worked in the Cannon Mills, Kannapolis.”
Hine gave the picture a title of his own:
“The logical conclusion of the laissez-faire policy.”
Outside the public school in Kannapolis, he photographed a group of children.
Every one of them, he wrote, said he or she had worked in the cotton mills.
The two smallest boys said they were ten.
In Concord, at the Cannon mill there,
he met a boy whose mother could not spell his name.
Hine wrote it down as Otie Honeycott. Otie said he had been doffing for two years.
Doffing meant pulling the full bobbins off the spinning frames
and putting empty ones on. It was quick work, for small hands.
And Hine photographed the houses.
“Some of the housing conditions of the workers,” he wrote,
“to contrast with the homes and gardens sometimes shown from the ‘show mills’ of the state.”
It would take a federal law, the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938,
to keep young children out of the mills for good.
We do not know what became of Herman Parker.
But we know what one child of the Cannon mills remembered, twenty-six years later.
In 1921, James Cannon died. His son Charles took over.
He was twenty-eight.
In 1928, Charles Cannon brought nine of the family's companies together into one:
Cannon Mills Company.
Under him, Kannapolis grew into one of the largest unincorporated towns in America.
There was no city government. The company was the government.
The fire insurance maps show it. Here is Kannapolis in 1926.
The mill, the railroad, and rows of small, identical houses, numbered like parts.
And here it is in 1943. The same streets, filled in.
Plant No. 1 has spread across the map, and the houses run out in every direction.
The company built the houses, owned them,
and rented them to the people who worked in the mill.
It built the YMCA, and gave the land and the buildings for much of the rest.
In September 1938, a writer for the government's Federal Writers' Project
sat on a front porch in Concord with a spinner named Alice Caudle.
Alice was forty-seven. She had worked for the Cannon Mills for more than thirty years.
She told the writer how it began.
“I was so little I had to stand on a box to reach my work.”
She was ten. She learned spinning, then spooling, then the new winding machines.
She was good at it, and she knew it.
“If I'd a-been a man no telling how far I'd-a gone.”
In 1938, her shift ran from seven in the morning to half past three.
For two full weeks of work, she was paid $31.
The rent on a company house was $6 a month.
That spring, the company held a supper in Kannapolis
for everyone who had worked twenty-five years or more. A car came to fetch her.
There was turkey, and white tablecloths finished at the company's own bleachery.
Charles Cannon made a speech, and gave out pins.
Alice remembered what he said.
“He told about the way young'uns used to stand on boxes to work — the way I done.”
When the office first called her in about it, she thought she was going to be fired.
When they handed her the ticket, she had a question.
“In all these thirty years this is the first time the Cannon Mill ever offered me anything —
are you right sure they're not a-going to take hit off my pay?”
And at the end, sitting on the porch, she said this.
“As long as I can work and talk and laugh, I'm happy.”
In August 1942, the First Lady came.
Eleanor Roosevelt asked to see what Cannon Mills provided for the people who worked there,
and toured the YMCA in Kannapolis.
By the 1940s, the town had its own city directory.
Page after page of names. And beside so many of them, the same employer.
A company town is a quiet town, until it isn't.
In September 1934, textile workers across the South walked out,
in the largest strike the industry had ever seen.
Mills were picketed. In some places, troops were sent in.
In Kannapolis, it would be sixty-five years before a union won a vote.
In 1974, Cannon workers voted on a union for the first time.
The union lost.
In 1985, they voted again. It lost again.
In 1991, and in 1997, there were more votes.
Both times, federal labor officials threw the results out,
finding that the company had intimidated union supporters.
Then, in June 1999, after twenty-five years of trying,
the workers of the Kannapolis mills voted the union in. Around five thousand of them.
It was called the greatest union victory in the history of southern textiles.
It came very late.
Charles Cannon died in April 1971.
For fifty years, he had run the mills, and the town, like a household.
Without him, the company was a large business like any other.
And large businesses can be bought.
In 1982, a California investor named David Murdock bought Cannon Mills,
with borrowed money.
Two years later, in 1984, Kannapolis finally became a city,
with a mayor and a council of its own.
Until then, it had been the largest unincorporated community in the United States.
Murdock soon sold the mills on, to Fieldcrest.
The workers' pension plan was closed, and its money moved into annuities with an insurance company.
When that insurer later failed, retired mill workers saw their pensions cut, by around 30%.
Fieldcrest Cannon was bought in turn, in 1997,
by a Texas company called Pillowtex.
Meanwhile, towels were being made more cheaply abroad.
Year by year, more of the towels and sheets on American shelves came from other countries.
In 2000, Pillowtex went bankrupt.
It came out of bankruptcy in 2002. It did not last.
On 30 July 2003, Pillowtex ran out of money, and stopped.
In Kannapolis and the counties around it,
4,340 people lost their jobs.
It was ninety-seven years since the first mill houses
went up on the farmland by the wagon road.
One dot for every job.
That was the day the town that made America's towels made its last one.
Plant No. 1 was enormous. Nearly six million square feet.
About the size of the Pentagon.
In 2005, the wreckers came.
In 2006, the last buildings and smokestacks were brought down with explosives.
The buyer of the land was the same man who had bought the company in 1982:
David Murdock.
Where the mill stood, he built a research campus,
for the science of food and health.
The old street names are still there. West Avenue. Main Street.
And the town has a council, a mayor and a city hall.
The things it waited nearly eighty years to have.
So what happened to Kannapolis?
A family built a town around a towel.
For almost a century, the town gave the mill its children, its parents, its whole working life.
When the mill went, the town stayed.
Herman Parker was six. Alice Caudle was ten.
The last workers walked out in 2003.
The looms are gone. The town is still here.
